contentItem.title: Pegula rallies past Navarro, sets Sabalenka showdown in 2026 US Open SFs
contentItem.shortTitle: Pegula rallies past Navarro; Sabalenka next in SFs
contentItem.metaTitle: Pegula rallies past Navarro, sets Sabalenka showdown in 2026 US Open SFs
contentItem.abstract: Jessica Pegula defeated Emma Navarro in an all-American quarterfinal clash at the US Open. The No. 3 seed advanced to face Aryna Sabalenka in the semifinals.

contentItem.jsx:
WHAT HAPPENED

In an all-American quarterfinal clash at the 2026 US Open, No. 3 seed Jessica Pegula beat No. 26 seed Emma Navarro, 3-6, 6-4, 6-3. Into the semifinals for the third straight year at her home Grand Slam, she will next meet world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka.

As she stepped inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, there was another opportunity in the offing for Pegula. She is one of four players vying for the title of No. 1 in the world, a crown she’d capture only if she wins the championship and Elena Rybakina fails to advance to the semifinals.

But the ever-steady Pegula has tended to sidestep chat about such matters. And on court, she always looks laser-focused on the task at hand: beating the player across the net.

Indeed, both Pegula and Navarro looked locked in to start the contest.

And there was no getting-to-know-you awkwardness to get out of the way. The two Americans had met four previous times. Pegula, age 32, had beaten Navarro, age 25, all four times—most recently in Cincinnati last month, on her way to the final, which she lost to Coco Gauff.

“Jess is really tough,” Navarro said after her Round 4 match here. “But there's always that time when you get over the hump and get the win.”

The first set opened with an exchange of service breaks, with both players facing, and saving, additional break points. And both players struggled to get their first serves in, which left them vulnerable to attacks on their second serves.

Pegula, in particular, looked rattled on serve, donating three double faults in a single game to slide to a 2-4 deficit (as compared to a total of 10 double faults across her first four matches).

A nearly nine-minute game ensued, which Navarro survived. After Pegula’s first efficient hold, at love, the younger American had the first set on her racquet. Navarro managed to claim the frame on her second set-point opportunity, 6-3.

The 50-minute set wasn’t a clean one for either player. Navarro racked up five double faults of her own (to just one ace), matching Pegula’s serving stats exactly. The difference maker? Pegula got her first serve in just 47% of the time and then won points behind her second serve 35% of the time. 

That Pegula is match tough is something of an understatement. She’s had a stellar 2026, claiming two titles, in Dubai and Charleston, and reaching the finals at three additional events, in Cincinnati, Washington, D.C., and Berlin—altogether racking up five finals appearances, the most of any WTA player. She also advanced to the semifinals at the 2026 Australian Open, where she lost to eventual champion Elena Rybakina.

For Navarro, who has been ranked as high as No. 8 in the world, 2026 has been a comeback year. She reached the semifinals here in 2024—her best-ever Slam showing—and the quarterfinals at the Australian Open in 2025 and Wimbledon in 2024.

But a medical condition (hypothyroidism) forced Navarro to take two months away from tennis this spring and after she returned in May, she dropped down to a WTA 125-level tournament.

“I feel like 80-85% of myself on and off the court,” Navarro said recently.

Pegula started the second set with vastly improved play. But, just like in the first set, the two players traded early breaks to keep the match on serve.

Long baseline rallies. Very little appetite for moving forward and shortening the points at the net. Seesaw games with multiple deuces. By the time the score leveled at 4-4, neither player was able to sustain an edge.

But then, down 4-5 and serving at 30-30, a nervous Navarro hit her first double fault of the set. That gave Pegula her first set point of the match. She took full advantage—and took the second set, 6-4.

A note on Pegula’s three-set record: She is 18-5 in third sets (compared to 11-9 for Navarro). That stat may have been the factor that gave the once-rattled Pegula the assurance she needed to stay composed and take control.

Up 3-2, Pegula put pressure on Navarro’s serve, breaking her to earn a 4-2 edge. That’s when the solid, steady Pegula started to shine. She held serve to stretch her lead to 5-2. And when she served next, on her second match point, Pegula converted, taking the set, 6-3, and the match.

“It was physical, it was human and I was fighting a lot of demons out there,” said Pegula in her on-court interview. “I do a great job of having a short-term memory,” she said, adding that she also had to “tell the negative me to just shut up.”

WHAT IT MEANS

The path gets no easier from here on out. No. 1 seed and two-time defending champion Sabalenka awaits in the semifinals, having dismissed Linda Noskova in a hard-fought quarterfinal contest, 7-6(1), 3-6, 7-6(7).

Pegula is 4-9 versus Sabalenka and has lost to her twice in Flushing, most recently in the semifinals at last year’s US Open. They also met in the 2024 US Open final, with Sabalenka taking the match, and the title, 7-5, 7-5.

On the other half of the draw loom the quarterfinalists who will be battling it out on Day 11. Playing in Ashe first are No. 2 seed Rybakina and Zheng Qinwen, ranked No. 121 in the world. To follow in Ashe is the match between American Coco Gauff, the No. 4 seed, and No. 5 seed Mirra Andreeva.

MATCH POINT

At age 32, Pegula ws also the oldest of the elite eight in New York—and if she takes the title here, she’d be the second-oldest player to win her first Grand Slam championship, following Flavia Pennetta, who was 33 when she claimed the crown at the 2015 US Open.
